method: Read the lesson end to end as a student first, then blind-solved all 47 items from the blind files only (misconception fields stripped before reading). Solves recorded here BEFORE opening any question file.
student_read_notes: Population figures: 'Between one and five million lived in the land that is now Canada and the United States, and about twenty million more lived in Mexico' - the 1-5m range is wide and 'twenty million more' is ambiguous (Mexico only, or Mexico plus Central America?). A student cannot tell what the 20m covers.
Ancestors 'walked from Asia... in waves stretching back as far as 40,000 years' - 40,000 years is at the high end; I doubt whether the books support it. Flag for book check.
Cahokia 'roughly the size of London at the same time' (1200s) - plausible but I have no way to check London's size from the lesson; flag for book check.

Tenochtitlan 'about 200,000 people, more than any city in Europe in 1500' - I doubt this: Paris in 1500 is often put near 200,000. 'More than any city in Europe' may overstate it. Flag for book check.
Iroquois League 'formed in the 1400s' - I know historians debate this (some say 1570, traditional date earlier). Flag for book check.
Worked item 2 part (b) model answer repeats itself: the second sentence restates the first (surplus feeds chiefs/priests and mound labor, said twice). Reads padded, not wrong.

Worked item 3 part (c): 'eight centuries after Cahokia's height' - 1907 minus ~1100 is 807 years, so 'eight centuries' is fine, but the lesson's Figure 1 is a 1907 photo of Monks Mound while the bank's MCQ set uses a Powell's Mound aerial photo - check the figure/stimulus match in adjudication.

The lesson never names the Inca except in worked item 1 and the SAQ 0001 stimulus; the closing check and narrative teach Aztec/Mexica only. A student meeting 'Inca' in SAQ 0001 part (a) has it in the stimulus, so it is answerable, but the lesson itself does not teach the Inca.

The lesson teaches 'West Africans' only in one sentence ('the meeting of three peoples') with no further content - thin, but the 47 questions do not test it, so it is a teaching thinness, not an unfair item.
Las Casas letter: 'he told the Spanish court that the islands held gentle people, gold, and spices' - 'spices' is a claim I cannot check from the lesson; flag for book check.

apush-mcq-0001.reason: Stimulus says he sent the account to Prince Philip to persuade the crown to stop the cruelty.

apush-mcq-0002.reason: He wrote to persuade; his figures are contested, so exact size cannot be taken from it. A is wrong (he wrote in Spanish), B wrong (1542), D wrong (Spanish friar).

apush-mcq-0003.reason: Conquest and forced labor after 1492 is the context; B wrong (no English colonies in 1542), C contradicts the passage, D wrong (slave trade had barely begun).

apush-mcq-0004.reason: A mound built centuries before contact shows large organized societies with labor for earthworks.

apush-mcq-0005.reason: Stimulus says Cahokia farmed maize and traded across the valley; complex societies existed before Columbus.

apush-mcq-0006.reason: Indigenous peoples built large permanent centers, as complex societies did elsewhere; A/D anachronistic, B unsupported.

apush-mcq-0007.reason: Map shows western lands as a separate landmass - recognized as a new continent, not Asia.

apush-mcq-0008.reason: Vespucci argued the lands were a new world; mapmakers agreed and named it for him.

apush-mcq-0009.reason: Ptolemy beside Vespucci frames new knowledge against classical geography - continuity and change.

apush-mcq-0010.reason: Table: third voyage 1498-1500, Trinidad and South American mainland near Venezuela.

apush-mcq-0011.reason: Four voyages over 12 years turned one crossing into sustained Spanish colonization.

apush-mcq-0012.reason: Line of Demarcation = Spain/Portugal division of claims (Tordesillas).

apush-mcq-0013.reason: Planting beans and maize in cleared fields shows farming was established and organized.

apush-mcq-0014.reason: Same people farm and hunt - they combined both food sources.

apush-mcq-0015.reason: De Bry never visited; engravings show Native life through European eyes with European assumptions.

apush-mcq-0016.reason: Books sold to European readers - scenes shaped to interest that audience.

apush-mcq-0017.reason: Classical poses show the artist's European point of view shaping the drawing.

apush-mcq-0018.reason: Two large cities in different regions, both maize-based - maize farming could support very large cities in different regions.

apush-mcq-0019.reason: Strongest test of food production as the cause: same environment, one farming and one foraging society - controls for environment.

apush-mcq-0020.reason: Maize surpluses fed large populations in both cities.

apush-mcq-0021.reason: Large populations plus mounds/plazas/temples/tribute - monumental building went with large populations.

apush-mcq-0022.reason: River valleys gave fertile floodplain soils for the maize surpluses chiefdoms depended on.

apush-mcq-0023.reason: The comparison's point: a large city grew in North America without Old World contact.

apush-mcq-0024.reason: Mounds/plazas/palisade show the society could organize large-scale building; they cannot tell names, language, exact yearly population, or beliefs.

apush-mcq-0025.reason: Gulf shells and Great Lakes copper reached Cahokia - faraway trade goods prove a trading hub.

apush-mcq-0026.reason: Three crops from one cleared field raised each field's yield.

apush-mcq-0027.reason: Three sisters agriculture sustained dense populations in the Northeast woodlands.

apush-mcq-0028.reason: Maize high, beans climbing, squash low - each crop uses a different layer of growing space.

apush-mcq-0029.reason: Farming alone is too narrow - farming, trade, and leadership together built Cahokia.

apush-mcq-0030.reason: Multi-story adobe dwellings in an arid landscape show a settled farming society suited to dry land.

apush-mcq-0031.reason: Compact adobe dwellings from local earth suit a dry climate; B/C/D are not in the image.

apush-mcq-0032.reason: Different environments, different economies - societies shaped their ways of life around their environments.

apush-mcq-0033.reason: Surpluses fed non-farming specialists (chiefs, priests) - the mechanism behind hierarchy.

apush-mcq-0034.reason: Pueblo peoples farmed adapted to the dry Southwest; the other pairings mismatch the table.

apush-mcq-0035.reason: Smaller and more mobile = foraging bands where maize agriculture was not practiced.

apush-mcq-0036.reason: Chinook settled and ranked without much farming - fishing/foraging can also support settled ranked societies.

apush-saq-0001.a: One characteristic is variety: the Americas held large cities such as Cahokia, empires such as the Aztec and the Inca, and many smaller farming and hunting societies, each adapted to its own region.
apush-saq-0001.b: Portuguese sailing down the west coast of Africa taught Europeans to use Atlantic winds and currents, and the search for a sea route to Asian spices gave them a reason to sail west, so by 1492 Europeans had both the skill and the motive to cross the ocean.
apush-saq-0001.c: European arrival brought conquest and forced labor, and diseases such as smallpox to peoples with no immunity, so Indigenous populations fell sharply and many societies lost people, land, and political independence.

apush-saq-0002.a: Columbus claims he found many islands full of gentle, quick-to-learn people, and that the islands held gold and spices, and that he took possession of the lands for the king and queen of Spain.
apush-saq-0002.b: Columbus wrote to report his findings to the Spanish court and win support and funding for more voyages.
apush-saq-0002.c: The letter was written to persuade the crown to support more voyages, so Columbus had reason to exaggerate the wealth and gentleness of the peoples; it is a European view written days after landing, not an Indigenous account.

apush-saq-0003.a: A north-south line runs through the Atlantic, and small flags mark the coasts claimed by Portugal and Spain.
apush-saq-0003.b: By 1502 Europeans knew the Atlantic coast of South America and the Caribbean and had mapped them as lands across the Atlantic, showing the world was wider than the old maps of Europe, Africa, and Asia.
apush-saq-0003.c: The dividing line and the flags show Spain and Portugal splitting the new lands between them, marking their rival claims to the Americas.

apush-saq-0004.a: In the arid Southwest, Pueblo peoples farmed dry land and built adobe villages, a way of life fitted to a dry climate.
apush-saq-0004.b: Maize farming in fertile river valleys produced surpluses that fed dense populations and supported chiefs, priests, and the labor that raised the mounds at Cahokia.
apush-saq-0004.c: Both the Pueblo peoples and the Iroquois villagers were settled farming peoples living in permanent villages.

apush-saq-0005.a: Harriot claims the people of Virginia planted maize, beans, and pumpkins in fields near their towns, and that their harvests fed them through the year.
apush-saq-0005.b: Harriot wrote to report on the land and its resources so as to encourage English settlement and investment in Virginia.
apush-saq-0005.c: Harriot wrote to promote the colony, so he may overstate how rich the land is; and he describes Virginia in 1585-86, nearly a century after first contact, so it is not evidence of pre-contact life untouched by Europeans.

apush-saq-0006.a: Native hunters on horseback chase bison across grassland.
apush-saq-0006.b: The horses show change after contact: Europeans brought horses to the Americas, and Plains peoples adopted mounted hunting, which transformed how they hunted bison.
apush-saq-0006.c: The image was made in the 1830s and 1840s, centuries after contact, and shows horseback hunting; before contact Plains peoples hunted on foot, so it cannot show pre-contact Plains life.

apush-saq-0007.a: As maize spread north, new towns and chiefdoms grew where farming could feed them.
apush-saq-0007.b: Trade networks carried maize seed, copper, shells, and stone across long distances, linking peoples who lived far apart.
apush-saq-0007.c: Both Mississippian chiefdoms and Mesoamerican societies were maize-farming societies that built large towns and cities ruled by chiefs or emperors supported by food surpluses.

apush-saq-0008.a: The mound shows Cahokia's people could organize the labor to raise a huge earthen structure, the mark of a large and organized society.
apush-saq-0008.b: Maize farming in the river valleys produced food surpluses that fed the workers and supported the chiefs who directed the building.
apush-saq-0008.c: The photograph was taken in 1907, about eight centuries after Cahokia's height, so it shows only the mound as it survived into modern times, not the city, the people, or the building work itself.

apush-leq-0001.thesis: Contact between Europeans and Indigenous peoples from 1491 to 1607 brought far-reaching change to the Americas - conquest, forced labor, epidemic disease, and the exchange of goods, crops, and animals transformed societies - though change was uneven and important continuities remained, as many Indigenous societies persisted, adapted, and kept their languages, farming, and political structures.
apush-leq-0001.outline: Context: diverse Indigenous societies before 1492 (Cahokia, Mexica, Iroquois) and European motives (sea route to Asian spices, gold, Christian mission). Evidence of change: disease (smallpox) devastating populations with no immunity; conquest of Mexica and Inca; encomienda and forced labor; Columbian Exchange (maize, horses, livestock, crops). Evidence of continuity: Indigenous farming (maize, three sisters) continued; Native peoples resisted and adapted; Spanish rule built on existing tribute and labor systems; regions with little direct contact changed slowly. Analysis: change was profound where contact was sustained but uneven across the continent.

apush-leq-0002.thesis: Native American societies adapted to their environments in distinct ways: where maize farming could feed dense populations, settled chiefdoms and villages grew, while in arid lands, grasslands, and rich fishing coasts, peoples developed irrigation farming, mobile hunting, or settled fishing villages - so environment shaped whether a society farmed, moved, or fished, and whether it built towns.
apush-leq-0002.outline: Context: maize spread north from Mexico over centuries; North America held many different environments. Evidence: Mississippian chiefdoms in river valleys (maize surpluses, Cahokia, mounds); Pueblo peoples in the arid Southwest (dry farming, irrigation, adobe); Iroquois in Northeast woodlands (three sisters, settled villages, League); Plains peoples (bison hunting on foot, mobile camps); Chinook on the Pacific coast (fishing, settled ranked villages without farming). Comparison: settled vs mobile, farming vs foraging routes to complexity.

apush-leq-0003.thesis: Maize agriculture transformed Native American societies to a great extent before 1492: it produced the food surpluses that supported dense populations, cities, chiefdoms, and long-distance trade across the Americas, though the transformation was uneven, since societies that did not adopt maize remained smaller and more mobile.
apush-leq-0003.outline: Context: maize was bred in Mesoamerica over thousands of years and spread north over centuries. Evidence: Cahokia (10,000-20,000 people, mounds, palisade); Tenochtitlan (about 200,000); Mississippian chiefdoms; three sisters farming in the Northeast; trade networks carrying maize seed, copper, shells, stone. Limit: Plains and Great Basin peoples stayed mobile foragers, and Pacific Northwest peoples built settled ranked villages from fishing, so maize was one road to complexity, not the only one.
